strengths: The paper addresses a practically important problem in automated software engineering: localizing issue-relevant files/classes/functions from natural-language bug reports, where agentic systems are often expensive and brittle.

The central empirical contribution is strong: SWERANK substantially improves over prior retrievers and reported agent-based baselines on SWE-Bench-Lite and LocBench, including meaningful gains at function-level Acc@10/15.

The SWELOC dataset construction is a valuable contribution. The paper gives a plausible pipeline from GitHub issues and PRs, excludes benchmark repositories, uses modified functions as positives, and applies consistency filtering plus hard-negative mining to reduce noise.

The retrieve-and-rerank formulation is simple, efficient, and well matched to the task. The cost analysis supports the claim that ranking-based localization can be much cheaper than closed-source LLM agents while remaining competitive or better.

The ablations on filtering threshold, dataset size, and transfer to multiple retriever/reranker backbones provide useful evidence that the dataset, not only the specific model choice, contributes to the improvements.
The paper is generally clear and well organized, with concrete comparisons across file, module, and function granularities.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate rather than high. The method largely combines standard bi-encoder contrastive retrieval, hard-negative mining, and listwise LLM reranking; the main new element is task-specific data construction and adaptation to issue localization.

The evaluation depends heavily on comparisons to agentic baselines whose numbers are taken from prior work. It is not fully clear that all systems use identical repository states, candidate spaces, localization definitions, retry budgets, context limits, and cost assumptions, which weakens the strength of the SOTA claim.

The dataset construction uses modified functions in PRs as positives, but this can be noisy: PRs may include refactors, tests, incidental edits, or multi-location changes not strictly required to fix the issue. The filtering helps, but may also bias the dataset toward cases already easy for the teacher embedding model.

Potential leakage is not fully ruled out. The paper excludes repositories in SWE-Bench and LocBench, but does not deeply discuss temporal leakage, duplicate issue text/code across forks, dependency copies, benchmark-adjacent repositories, or overlap through pretrained model data.

The reranker training objective only supervises the positive identifier as the first output rather than a full ranking. This is pragmatic, but the paper does not analyze whether the generated full ranking is well calibrated beyond top positions or how it behaves when multiple functions are relevant.

The ablations are helpful but incomplete. Stronger controls would include comparisons to static sequential reranking, oracle retriever recall ceilings, random/teacher-negative variants, BM25 plus the same reranker, and a retriever trained without consistency filtering from CodeRankEmbed to isolate teacher-model bias.

Reproducibility is not yet sufficient for a top score. The paper says code, data, and models will be released, but the manuscript currently lacks a valid release link and many implementation details such as prompts, exact candidate formatting, preprocessing scripts, and benchmark evaluation scripts are not fully specified.

The paper focuses on localization accuracy but does not show downstream patch-generation impact. Since the motivation is automated repair, evidence that SWERANK improves actual fix rates or developer workflows would make the significance much stronger.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and practical problem: localizing relevant files/classes/functions for real-world software issues, where cheaper alternatives to multi-step LLM agents would be valuable.

The proposed SWELOC dataset construction is a plausible source of task-specific supervision, and the paper includes useful analyses of filtering strength, data size, and transfer to several retriever/reranker backbones.

The empirical results are numerically strong on SWE-Bench-Lite and LocBench, especially for the trained retrievers relative to generic code/text embedding baselines, and the cost motivation is compelling if the setup is valid.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is limited: SWERANK is a standard retrieve-and-rerank pipeline with contrastive bi-encoder training and a listwise LLM reranker. The main novelty is the dataset, but the dataset construction and validation are not sufficiently rigorous for the strength of the claims.

The automatically derived supervision is noisy and potentially biased. Treating PR-modified functions as positives assumes all relevant locations correspond exactly to changed functions and that unmodified functions are irrelevant. This is particularly problematic for issues spanning multiple files/functions, refactors, tests, or behavioral changes where the true localization set is ambiguous.

Data leakage and contamination are insufficiently addressed. The paper excludes repositories from SWE-Bench and LocBench, but does not provide a convincing audit for duplicate issues, forks, copied code, transitive repository overlap, or pretraining contamination in the large embedding/LLM backbones. Given the benchmark sizes, this is a major concern.

The evaluation is too narrow for the claims. SWE-Bench-Lite is reduced from 300 to 274 examples by excluding cases without existing modified functions, which favors the proposed function-ranking formulation. There is no downstream patch-generation evaluation showing that the localized results actually improve repair success.

Comparisons to agentic systems are not fully convincing. The paper relies on numbers from prior work rather than a controlled rerun under the same input/output constraints, and compares single-shot rankers to agents without carefully normalizing candidate spaces, allowed context, output formats, latency, or failure modes.

Some headline claims are overstated. For example, the paper presents GPT-4.1 reranking results that outperform SWERANK on several metrics, yet the text still makes broad SOTA and closed-source comparison claims. The cost analysis also omits training cost, indexing cost, hardware amortization, and realistic deployment costs for 7B/32B rerankers.

Important implementation and reproducibility details are missing or weak. The abstract says code/data/models will be released, but the link is blank in the manuscript. The final filtered SWELOC size is unclear, prompts and candidate construction at evaluation time are underspecified, and the full benchmark preprocessing/evaluation scripts are not described enough to reproduce the exact numbers.

The reranker training objective is questionable for multi-location localization: it trains the model to output only one positive identifier among sampled candidates, while evaluation often requires recovering all relevant locations. The paper does not adequately analyze this mismatch or cases with multiple modified functions.

Ablations are incomplete. The paper does not isolate the contribution of dataset scale versus backbone strength versus reranker size in a fully controlled way, nor does it compare against simpler strong baselines such as BM25 plus learned reranking, issue-title/log ablations, repository-path/name features, or non-LLM cross-encoders.

Writing and polish are below top-tier standard in places, with grammatical errors, inconsistent terminology, and imprecise claims. This is secondary to the technical concerns, but it reinforces the impression that the submission is not yet mature.

strengths: The paper addresses an important bottleneck in automated software engineering: localizing issue-relevant code before patch generation. The motivation is clear, and the proposed ranking framing is a practical alternative to expensive multi-step agentic localization.

SWELOC is a valuable contribution: it is large-scale, derived from real GitHub issues and PRs, filtered to avoid overlap with SWE-Bench and LocBench, and designed specifically around the mismatch between verbose issue reports and code snippets.

The empirical results are strong. SWERANK improves over prior retrievers and agent-based baselines on SWE-Bench-Lite and LocBench across file, module, and function localization, with especially compelling function-level Acc@10/Acc@15 results.

The paper includes useful analyses beyond headline scores: filtering threshold ablations, training-data size trends, transfer to multiple retriever backbones, reranker finetuning results, and inference cost comparisons.
The method is technically simple but well matched to the problem. The retrieve-and-rerank design is scalable, efficient, and likely easier to deploy than tool-using agents.
The paper is generally clear and well organized, with enough training detail in the appendix to understand model choices, hyperparameters, and reranker supervision.
weaknesses: The core modeling contribution is incremental: the architecture is a standard bi-encoder plus listwise LLM reranker, and much of the novelty rests on task-specific data construction rather than a fundamentally new method.

The dataset labels are noisy by construction. Treating modified functions as positives and all unmodified functions as negatives can miss relevant context, helper functions, configuration files, newly added functions, or issue-relevant code that was not changed in the final PR.

The evaluation excludes SWE-Bench-Lite examples where no existing function was modified, which is reasonable for the chosen formulation but narrows the claim. The paper should be more explicit about how this affects comparability to agentic systems that can localize files or generate new code.

The comparison to agent-based methods is persuasive but not fully controlled. Several agent results are taken from prior work, and it is not always clear whether all methods use identical filtering, repository snapshots, localization granularity, and candidate definitions.

The cost analysis is useful but incomplete: it emphasizes inference API cost while largely omitting embedding/index construction, reranker serving assumptions, hardware amortization, latency, and the substantial training cost of the 7B/32B models.
The paper would be stronger with a downstream patch-generation evaluation showing that improved localization actually improves repair success, not only localization metrics.

Reproducibility is promised but not yet demonstrated in the manuscript; the code/data/model release link appears incomplete, and the large training setup may be difficult for many groups to reproduce.
The work is limited to Python repositories and benchmarks; it is unclear how well SWELOC and SWERANK transfer to other programming languages, monorepos, or industrial codebases.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: efficient localization of code locations from real-world issue descriptions, which is a key bottleneck for automated software repair.
Introduces SWELOC, a large automatically curated issue-localization dataset, and uses it to train both dense retrievers and listwise rerankers.

Empirical results are strong on SWE-Bench-Lite and LocBench, with consistent gains over prior retrievers and competitive or better results than agentic baselines at much lower reported inference cost.

The paper includes useful analyses beyond headline metrics: data filtering and size ablations, retriever/reranker transfer to other backbones, issue complexity breakdowns, lexical/semantic overlap analysis, multilingual generalization, and downstream repair impact.
The method is conceptually simple and practical: a retrieve-and-rerank formulation is easier to deploy and reason about than multi-step agentic localization.
weaknesses: Novelty is somewhat incremental: the core method is a standard bi-encoder retriever plus listwise LLM reranker, with the main contribution being task-specific data construction and training rather than a fundamentally new modeling approach.

The automatically constructed supervision is noisy: all modified functions in a PR are treated as positives, but patches may include refactors, cleanup, tests, or collateral edits that are not necessary localization targets. This limits confidence in the dataset labels.

The consistency filtering procedure uses a pretrained retriever to decide which examples are retained, which may bias the dataset toward examples already solvable by embedding similarity and may underrepresent harder issue-code reasoning cases.

The comparison with agentic methods is not fully apples-to-apples. Agents may optimize different interaction protocols and output formats, while SWERANK is evaluated as a ranking system over extracted functions with precomputed candidates.

Cost and latency claims are promising but somewhat incomplete: they emphasize inference reranking while largely excluding training cost, embedding precomputation, indexing, hardware assumptions, and the practical cost of very long reranker prompts.

Reproducibility is not fully convincing from the manuscript alone: the first-page code/model availability footnote appears incomplete, and key implementation details such as exact prompts, candidate construction, truncation effects, and benchmark preprocessing could be more explicit.

Evaluation relies mainly on ground-truth modified locations from accepted patches; it does not deeply analyze whether retrieved locations are semantically sufficient for alternative valid fixes or whether failures arise from missing context outside functions.

strengths: The paper targets an important and practical problem: localizing relevant code for real GitHub issues, which is a central bottleneck for automated software repair and developer-assistance systems.

SWELOC is a potentially valuable contribution: the dataset construction pipeline is clearly motivated, reasonably large-scale, and tailored to the mismatch between conventional code retrieval queries and verbose issue reports.

The proposed retrieve-and-rerank formulation is simple but effective. The paper reports strong gains over BM25, prior code retrievers, large embedding models, and several agentic localization baselines on SWE-Bench-Lite and LocBench.

The empirical section is broader than average: it includes file/module/function localization, retriever and reranker comparisons, data filtering and data size analyses, model-family transfer experiments, cost/latency discussion, downstream repair impact, complexity breakdowns, and multilingual evaluation in the appendix.
The efficiency argument is meaningful. A single-shot ranking system that approaches or exceeds agent-based localization accuracy at much lower inference cost is practically attractive.
weaknesses: The core method is technically incremental. SWERANK is mostly a standard bi-encoder plus listwise LLM reranker trained on task-specific data with known contrastive learning and hard-negative mining techniques; the main novelty is dataset construction and application rather than a new modeling idea.

The supervision signal is noisy and only partially justified. Treating all modified functions in a PR as positives and all unmodified functions as negatives can mislabel incidental edits, helper changes, refactors, and latent relevant code. The consistency filter mitigates this but also biases the dataset toward cases already retrievable by an existing embedding model.

The evaluation relies heavily on localization metrics derived from patch edits. This is useful, but it does not fully establish that the localized code is causally responsible for the issue or sufficient for repair. The downstream repair improvement is modest, and oracle localization only slightly improves Pass@1, weakening the practical impact claim.

Comparisons to agentic systems are not fully apples-to-apples. Agents may use different budgets, tools, stopping criteria, models, and output formats, while SWERANK is optimized directly for the localization metric. The paper would benefit from a more controlled reimplementation or standardized inference protocol.

The cost analysis is somewhat under-specified and potentially optimistic. Pre-computation, indexing, hardware amortization, reranking candidate count, and local serving assumptions are not analyzed in enough detail to support strong claims about real deployment cost.

Reproducibility is weaker than it should be for a dataset/model paper. The manuscript includes training hyperparameters, but the code/model URL footnote appears blank, and important details such as exact repository filtering, deduplication thresholds, issue-PR linking heuristics, prompt templates, and benchmark preprocessing are not fully specified in the main text.

The paper would benefit from more direct error analysis. The current breakdowns by complexity and overlap are useful, but they do not deeply analyze concrete failure modes such as multi-file architectural bugs, misleading stack traces, test-only edits, renamed functions, dependency-related fixes, or cases requiring dynamic execution.

Some claims are overstated relative to the evidence, especially broad claims of state-of-the-art performance and generalization. The experiments are strong enough to show useful benchmark gains, but not enough to establish a broadly superior replacement for agentic localization in realistic development workflows.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: efficient software issue localization as a prerequisite for automated repair. The framing is compelling, especially against costly multi-step agentic systems.

The proposed SWELOC dataset is a valuable contribution. It is large-scale, derived from real GitHub issues and patches, excludes overlap with SWE-Bench/LocBench, and includes thoughtful consistency filtering and hard-negative mining.

The empirical results are strong. SWERANK improves over prior retrievers, rerankers, and agent-based methods on SWE-Bench-Lite and LocBench, with gains shown at file, module, and function granularity.

The evaluation is broad and well supported by ablations: data filtering, data size, retriever/reranker transfer, model capacity, negative mining, multilingual generalization, issue complexity, overlap analysis, and downstream repair impact.
The efficiency argument is convincing: the retrieve-and-rerank formulation gives substantially lower inference cost and latency than agentic localization while maintaining or improving accuracy.
The methodology is simple but effective, making the work likely to be useful to practitioners and easy to build upon.
weaknesses: The core modeling approach is largely standard retrieve-and-rerank with task-specific fine-tuning; the main novelty is the dataset and empirical positioning rather than a fundamentally new algorithm.

The SWELOC construction uses modified functions as positives, which can be noisy: patches may include refactoring, test-support changes, incidental edits, or code locations that are changed but not semantically responsible for the issue.

The consistency filtering uses an existing embedding model to select training examples, which may bias the dataset toward examples that are already retrievable by semantic similarity and underrepresent harder localization cases.

The comparison to agentic systems is persuasive but not perfectly apples-to-apples: agents may use broader repository context, iterative exploration, and different operating constraints, while SWERANK relies on candidate extraction and large reranking contexts.
The evaluation excludes SWE-Bench-Lite instances without modified existing functions, which is reasonable for function localization but narrows the claim of general software issue localization.

Reproducibility would depend heavily on the release quality of SWELOC, code, exact preprocessing, candidate extraction, and trained checkpoints; the paper states availability, but the extracted manuscript does not clearly show a complete artifact link.
Cost and latency analysis is useful but somewhat idealized, since it assumes precomputed embeddings and does not fully discuss indexing, candidate extraction, hardware requirements, or training cost.
